name: Imagined contact
statement: Imagining a positive conversation with a member of an out-group is said to improve attitudes and contact intentions towards that group.
meaning: The task takes about a minute. A participant is told to picture meeting a stranger from some other group and to imagine the encounter going well, then usually writes down what was imagined. A control group pictures something neutral, often an outdoor scene. Attitudes, emotions, intentions or behaviour towards the group are measured straight afterwards. The claim is causal and it is about mental simulation alone, with no meeting, no stranger and no room. That is what separates it from the contact hypothesis, which concerns people who have actually met. The two rest on separate literatures, and one of them is far larger.

origin.who: Rhiannon N. Turner, Richard J. Crisp and Emily Lambert
origin.note: Three experiments. Young participants who imagined talking to an elderly person showed less bias than participants who imagined an outdoor scene, and less than participants who merely thought about elderly people, which the authors read as ruling out priming. In the third, heterosexual men who imagined talking to a homosexual man evaluated homosexual men more positively, and reduced intergroup anxiety mediated the change. Crisp and Turner set the idea out for a general readership in American Psychologist in 2009, and that article is what drew the published objections.

evidence:
The study the replicators took is Husnu and Crisp's, published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology in 2010. Klein and colleagues describe its first experiment this way. British non-Muslim participants either imagined interacting with a British Muslim stranger or imagined walking outdoors. They imagined for one minute and described their thoughts for another, then rated their interest and willingness to interact with British Muslims on four items. Kvarven, Strømland and Johannesson record that experiment as N = 33 with d = 0.86, standard error 0.365, 95% CI [0.145, 1.575], p = 0.018. Thirty-three people is the whole of the original evidence for the effect that was then tested on 6,336.

The wider case rests on Miles and Crisp's meta-analysis, published in Group Processes & Intergroup Relations in 2014. Its abstract reports more than 70 studies and an overall d+ = 0.35 across attitudes, emotions, intentions and behaviour, significant among published and unpublished studies alike. It also reports the effect as equally strong on explicit and implicit attitude measures, stronger on intentions than on attitudes, stronger for children than for adults, and stronger the more elaboration the imagining instructions demanded. Valence, the type of control condition and time spent imagining made no difference. Only that abstract was obtainable.

replication.headline: Thirty-six samples and 6,336 people put the effect at about a seventh of the original: weighted d = 0.13, 99% CI [0.07, 0.19], with 4 of the 36 samples reaching significance in the right direction.
replication.detail:
Klein and 50 colleagues ran 13 effects across 36 samples and 6,344 participants. For imagined contact their Table 2 gives an original of d = 0.86, 95% CI [.14, 1.57], against a median replication of 0.12. The unweighted mean was 0.10, 99% CI [0.00, 0.19], and the weighted mean 0.13, 99% CI [0.07, 0.19], t = 5.05, df 6,334, p < .001. Four of the 36 samples found the effect on their own, one found it reversed, and 31 found nothing. Results varied little between sites: Q = 45.87 on 35 degrees of freedom, p = 0.10, I² = 0.206, and neither country nor laboratory-versus-online moved the estimate by a measurable share of variance. The paper's own summary is that imagined contact 'showed weak support for replicability', and its discussion lists it among the effects the original studies overestimated.

Kvarven, Strømland and Johannesson matched 15 meta-analyses to multi-laboratory replications of the same effects, and imagined contact is one pair. Taking the 32 intentions effects from Miles and Crisp, 2,076 participants in all, they get d = 0.459, 95% CI [0.324, 0.594] against the replication's 0.13. The gap is 0.329, standard error 0.073, p < 0.001. Correcting the meta-analysis for publication bias narrows it without closing it: trim and fill gives 0.339 [0.194, 0.483], a three-parameter selection model gives 0.293 [0.092, 0.494], and PET-PEESE gives -0.354 [-0.904, 0.196]. Across all 15 pairs, meta-analytic estimates averaged almost three times the replication estimates and differed from them in 12 cases.

Smaller tests since have gone both ways. Hoffarth and Hodson found imagined contact improved heterosexual participants' emotions and attitudes towards gay men where previous contact had been infrequent, N = 261, and found nothing at all with Muslims as the target, N = 320. Firat and Ataca tested 335 Turkish undergraduates on prejudice towards Kurds and Syrians and report that imagined contact did not reduce it, explicitly or implicitly, with no moderation by in-group identification.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Ratliff, K. A., Vianello, M., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142-152.

limits:
Two documents at the centre of this could not be opened. Husnu and Crisp's article is closed at the publisher, and every repository copy of it sits on a host this project's network refused, so nothing here comes from its own text. Klein and colleagues say its first experiment compared imagined contact against imagining an outdoor scene. Crisp and Turner's 2012 review describes the same experiment as a comparison of standard against elaborated imagined contact. Both descriptions cannot be the design of one two-condition test, and the paper that would settle it was not read. Miles and Crisp's meta-analysis was likewise unobtainable beyond its abstract, so its overall d+ = 0.35 is quoted from that abstract, and the per-outcome and moderator estimates behind it are not on this page. The figures for its intentions subset come from Kvarven and colleagues' supplementary tables rather than from the meta-analysis itself.

The published objections could not be read either. Lee and Jussim's 'Back in the real world' and Bigler and Hughes's 'Reasons for skepticism about the efficacy of simulated social contact interventions' are two-page comments in American Psychologist, both closed, with no abstract at PubMed or Crossref. What they argued is reported here only as Crisp and Turner summarise it in their own review, which is the answering side of the argument. Dermody, Jones and Cumming's paper, whose title reports a failure with male homosexuals as the target, exists as a Crossref record with no abstract and was not read.

The outcome in the replicated study is self-reported willingness to interact, collected within minutes of the imagining task. Crisp and Turner name that risk themselves, writing that participants may guess the rationale and answer to the perceived expectations of the experimenter, and they argue that effects on implicit measures rule the explanation out. Miles and Crisp's abstract reports explicit and implicit measures as equally affected. No study located here tested whether the effect on intentions survives a delay of weeks, and no field trial of the technique was read.

Searching ran across Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the open web. Publisher and repository copies at Sage, Elsevier, Hogrefe, Durham, Sussex and figshare were all refused by the network rather than missing.
misreadings:
The commonest error is lending this the credit of the contact hypothesis. Pettigrew and Tropp's meta-analysis covers 713 independent samples from 515 studies of people who had actually met, and finds that contact typically reduces prejudice. They report that the finding survives tests for participant selection and publication bias, with the more rigorous studies yielding the larger effects. Imagining a stranger is a different manipulation with a different evidence base, and the multi-laboratory estimate for it is d = 0.13. Nothing in the face-to-face literature bears on whether the imagined version works.

The second error is treating the meta-analytic 0.35 as the size a school or workplace exercise would deliver. It is the average of the published and unpublished imagined-contact literature, and the one estimate produced without publication bias, from 36 samples run to a common protocol, is a quarter of that. Read the two together and the honest summary is a small effect on what people say they intend, not a tool for prejudice.

The third error runs the other way. Many Labs 1 did not find nothing: its pooled interval clears zero at 99%, and the paper says so in the same breath as calling the support weak. Each laboratory contributed a small sample, so the 31 null results are what an effect of that size looks like when it is chopped into 36 pieces, and counting them as 31 failures overstates the case.

The fourth is forgetting what the outcome measure is. In the replicated design the participant imagines a friendly encounter and then, minutes later, rates how willing they are to have one.

sources.text: Turner, R. N., Crisp, R. J., & Lambert, E. (2007). Imagining intergroup contact can improve intergroup attitudes. Group Processes & Intergroup Relations, 10(4), 427-441. The founding demonstration. Read as its Crossref abstract only.

Crisp, R. J., & Turner, R. N. (2009). Can imagined interactions produce positive perceptions? Reducing prejudice through simulated social contact. American Psychologist, 64(4), 231-240. The article that put the technique before a general readership and drew the two published comments. Verified as a Crossref record only.

Husnu, S., & Crisp, R. J. (2010). Elaboration enhances the imagined contact effect. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 46(6), 943-950. The study Many Labs 1 replicated. Closed at the publisher and unreachable at every repository copy; not read for this entry.

Klein, R. A., Ratliff, K. A., Vianello, M., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A 'Many Labs' replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3), 142-152. Tables 2 and 3 and the design description read from the accepted manuscript at LSE Research Online; the abstract was read again at Crossref.

Miles, E., & Crisp, R. J. (2014). A meta-analytic test of the imagined contact hypothesis. Group Processes & Intergroup Relations, 17(1), 3-26. Paywalled, with repository copies unreachable; only the abstract at Crossref was read.

Kvarven, A., Strømland, E., & Johannesson, M. (2020). Comparing meta-analyses and preregistered multiple-laboratory replication projects. Nature Human Behaviour, 4(4), 423-434. The imagined-contact figures here come from Supplementary Tables 1 to 4 and 9 to 12 of the supplementary information PDF; the main text is paywalled, and its abstract was read at PubMed.

Hoffarth, M. R., & Hodson, G. (2016). Who needs imagined contact? Replication attempts examining previous contact as a potential moderator. Social Psychology, 47(2), 118-124. Read as its Crossref abstract only.
Firat, M., & Ataca, B. (2020). When does imagined contact reduce prejudice? Social Psychology, 51(4), 254-266. Read as its Crossref abstract only.

Dermody, N., Jones, M. K., & Cumming, S. R. (2013). The failure of imagined contact in reducing explicit and implicit out-group prejudice toward male homosexuals. Current Psychology, 32(3), 261-274. Located as a Crossref record with no abstract; not read, and no claim here rests on it.

Crisp, R. J., & Turner, R. N. (2012). The imagined contact hypothesis. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 46, 125-182. The proponents' own review, read as the author manuscript at Queen's University Belfast. Cited here for its account of the two American Psychologist comments and of the demand-characteristics objection.
Lee, Y.-T., & Jussim, L. (2010). Back in the real world. American Psychologist, 65(2), 130-131. A comment on Crisp and Turner. Closed, with no abstract at PubMed or Crossref; not read.

Bigler, R. S., & Hughes, J. M. (2010). Reasons for skepticism about the efficacy of simulated social contact interventions. American Psychologist, 65(2), 132-133, with a reply at 133-135. Closed, with no abstract at PubMed or Crossref; not read.

Pettigrew, T. F., & Tropp, L. R. (2006). A meta-analytic test of intergroup contact theory. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 90(5), 751-783. The face-to-face literature this effect is confused with. Read as its PubMed abstract only, which is why no pooled estimate from it appears here.
